notes.title: Chapter map: Data model & object semantics
notes.html:
Everything here follows from two facts: every value is an object on the heap, and a name is only a label on one. Read each arrow as a sentence: is vs == built on names & binding.

Green = CORE, blue = SUPPORTING, yellow = BREADTH, grey = another chapter (dashed edges).

Reading order:00 execution model01 names02 is vs ==03 mutable defaults06 copy04 dunders04a eq / hash08 ordering05 slots07 truthiness
  • The one big idea: there are two branches. Names (01 → 02, 03, 06): assignment never copies, so every "why did that change?" bug is two names on one object. Dunders (04 → 04a, 05, 07, 08): syntax is a call to a method looked up on the type, so defining the method buys the syntax and its contract.
  • The two most-confused pairs: mutation vs rebinding (01: all names see a mutation, no other name sees a rebind) · is vs == (02: same object vs same value, and == runs your code).
  • Ten minutes before an interview: the TL;DR and Flow lines of 01, 03 and 04a, then the Break it in 03 (the shared default list).
  • Cross-chapter: reference counting (every binding moves a refcount) · dict internals (where the eq/hash contract is enforced).

No decision tree: these notes build on each other rather than being alternatives to choose between. The one real choice in the chapter (assignment vs shallow vs deep copy) lives inside 06.

notes.title: The CPython Execution Model
notes.html:
References

Execution model · dis — bytecode disassembler · Compiled Python files · GfG: Understanding the execution of a Python program

TL;DR

CPython compiles source to bytecode, then interprets the bytecode. Compiled ahead of execution, never ahead of time to native code.

Flow:.py sourceparser builds the ASTcompiler emits a code objectimported? cache it as .pyceval loop runs one opcode at a timeevery value is a heap object with a type and a refcount

Recall

Prompt Answer
Compiled or interpreted? Both, in sequence: compiled to bytecode, then the bytecode is interpreted.
What is in __pycache__? Cached bytecode for imported modules, tagged with the interpreter version.
Why is a pure-Python loop slow? Every opcode pays evaluation-loop dispatch; there's no native-code step.

The idea

Where did the __pycache__/helpers.cpython-312.pyc in your project come from? Nobody asked for it. CPython wrote it because it compiled helpers.py before running any of it. You can see the same output for any function:

import dis
def add(a, b): return a + b
dis.dis(add)          # → LOAD_FAST a · LOAD_FAST b · BINARY_OP (+) · RETURN_VALUE
add.__code__.co_consts  # → literals already extracted into a table before any call

Those aren't CPU instructions. They're instructions for a stack machine inside CPython, and an evaluation loop executes them one at a time. So both halves of "compiled or interpreted?" are true, in order.

Everything those instructions touch is a heap object with a type pointer and a refcount. There are no primitives: 10, add, int and the module are all objects. That uniformity buys introspection, decorators and monkey-patching, and costs you boxing: a list of a million ints is far larger than an array of them.

The trade: Python gives up native-code speed and unboxed data, and gets back a uniform object model you can inspect and rewrite at runtime.

How it works

The pipeline runs on the first import of each module:

Caching is per-module and version-tagged. Only imported modules get a .pyc. The script you run directly is compiled in memory and thrown away. Bytecode isn't stable across releases, so the filename carries cpython-XY, and CPython checks the source's mtime and size before reusing the cache.

The evaluation loop is where frames live. In CPython, each call pushes a frame holding the locals array, value stack and instruction pointer. A traceback prints that chain, and a suspended generator keeps its frame instead of dropping it.

Memory is refcounting first, GC second. A count rises on binding and falls on rebinding or scope exit. At zero the object is freed immediately, so CPython's memory behaviour is predictable. The cyclic collector exists only for reference cycles that refcounting can never free.

Code

Frames and implementation details are inspectable objects, which is what makes the rest of this vault testable at the REPL:

import sys

print(sys.implementation.name, sys.version_info[:2])   # → cpython (3, 12)

def outer():
    f = sys._getframe()                 # the live frame a traceback would walk
    return f.f_code.co_name, f.f_back.f_code.co_name
print(outer())                          # → ('outer', '<module>')

Interview

30-second answer: Both, in order. CPython compiles source to bytecode, an instruction set for its own stack machine, not machine code, and caches it in __pycache__ for imported modules. Then the evaluation loop interprets that bytecode one opcode at a time. There's no step to native code, which is where the per-instruction overhead comes from. So the performance fix is to move hot loops into C (NumPy, extensions), not to micro-optimise Python.

Q · Mechanism — What happens between saving a .py file and a line of it running? The source is parsed into an AST, and the compiler emits a code object: bytecode, a constants table and the local-variable layout. An imported module's code is cached as a version-tagged .pyc, validated against source mtime and size on the next import. __main__ is never cached. Each call then pushes a frame, and the loop dispatches opcodes against it, operating on refcounted heap objects.

Compare

CPython PyPy
Execution eval loop interprets bytecode tracing JIT compiles hot paths to native code
Wins on reference behaviour, C-API compatibility long-running pure-Python loops
Loses on tight numeric loops in pure Python short scripts; C-extension-heavy code
Memory refcounting + generational cyclic GC tracing GC, no refcounts

Pitfalls

  • "Python executes source line by line"
    The whole module compiles to bytecode first, then the bytecode runs.
    ↳ Proof: a SyntaxError on line 200 stops line 1 from ever running.
    ↳ Interview: "line by line" invites the __pycache__ follow-up.
  • "Python always runs the .pyc"
    .pyc caches imported modules only.
    ↳ Why: a script run directly is compiled in memory every time and never written out.
    ↳ So: moving logic into an imported module is what saves the compile step.
  • Not the same as a language property
    ↳ Difference: "compiled vs interpreted" describes an implementation (CPython, PyPy, Jython), not Python.
    ↳ Also: bytecode is not machine code; it targets CPython's own VM, so it's portable across CPUs but not across Python versions.
  • Don't ship .pyc without sources to hide code.
    ↳ Why: bytecode decompiles back to readable Python, and the files only load on the exact minor version that wrote them.
    ↳ Result: no secrecy, and a brittle deployment.
  • 🔖 Version: opcode names change between releases (BINARY_ADD → BINARY_OP in 3.11).
    ↳ So: run dis on your own interpreter; free-threaded 3.13+ builds (PEP 703) also change how refcounting works.

Connections

Path:execution modelnames & bindingthe eval loopreference counting
  • Used by names & binding: STORE_FAST is the opcode that binds a name.
  • Used by the eval loop: the in-depth view of the last box in the flowchart.
  • Used by the GIL: one shared heap of refcounted objects is why the lock exists.
  • Contrasts with PyPy's tracing JIT (the Compare table): same language, native code for hot paths.
  • Same idea elsewhere: Java compiles to JVM bytecode, then interprets it and JIT-compiles the hot paths.

notes.title: Names, Binding & Assignment
notes.html:
References

Execution model: naming and binding · Assignment statements · Augmented assignment · Ned Batchelder: Facts and myths about Python names and values · Real Python: Variables in Python

TL;DR

Assignment binds a name to an object; it never copies. Mutation changes the object (all names see it); rebinding moves one name (no other name sees it).

Flow:b = aLOAD_FAST pushes a's pointerSTORE_FAST writes it into b's slotone object, two namesb.append() changes it for bothb = b + [5] builds a new list and moves only b

Recall

Prompt Answer
What is a variable, mechanically? A namespace slot holding a pointer to a heap object, not a box of bytes.
Does b = a ever copy? Never. Same pointer in a second slot, so id(a) == id(b).
Rebinding vs mutation? Rebinding repoints one name; mutation changes the shared object for every name.
Pass-by-value or pass-by-reference? Neither: pass-by-object-reference. The reference is copied, the object shared.
Why doesn't n += 1 affect an alias of an int? int has no __iadd__; falls back to __add__ and rebinds.
Draw by hand: mutation vs rebinding Mutation: two names → one changed list. Rebinding: only b's arrow moves, to a new list.

The idea

When you write b = a, what exactly got written where? Not conceptually, literally:

a = [1, 2, 3]
b = a                 # ① copy the pointer into b's slot
id(a) == id(b)        # → True
b.append(4); a        # → [1, 2, 3, 4]

Two names, one address, so one list. The second line built nothing; it copied the pointer in a's slot into b's slot. That costs one machine word whether the object is three ints or a 400 MB DataFrame. By default, assignment shares, and every name bound to an object is a live window onto it.

Now the line that looks like more of the same:

b = b + [5]           # ② build a new list, overwrite b's slot only
a, id(a) == id(b)     # → ([1, 2, 3, 4], False)

a didn't move. b.append(4) mutated the object, so every name saw it. b = b + [5] rebound the name: it built a new list and overwrote one slot. Argument passing is the same rule. The callee gets its own name for your object, so lst.append(99) reaches you and lst = [] doesn't. That's why the precise term is pass-by-object-reference (call-by-sharing).

The trade: O(1) assignment and free sharing of any object, in exchange for deciding at every boundary whether you meant to share.

How it works

Two assignments, two paths through the eval loop:

The rules behind those two paths:

Rule What actually happens
A name is a slot In CPython a function local is a numbered entry in the frame's fast-locals array, fixed at compile time; a module or class name is a key in a real dict. Assignment writes a PyObject * there and bumps the refcount, so the object outlives del a while b holds it.
The object is never consulted STORE_FAST calls no method on the list and can't know it's aliased, so nothing inside a class can stop it being shared: sharing happens in the caller's namespace.
+= is the one exception It compiles to an in-place BINARY_OP, so the type answers through __iadd__: a list mutates and returns itself; an int has none, falls back to __add__ and stores a new object (see Break it).
Every binding statement works this way def, class, import and for all bind names. def f(): … builds a function object and binds f, which is why a decorator is just f = deco(f).

Code

At a boundary you decide to share or own. Two tools for the same hazard:

from dataclasses import dataclass, replace

DEFAULTS = {"timeout": 30, "retries": 3}    # module-level, shared by everyone

def make_config(overrides: dict) -> dict:
    cfg = dict(DEFAULTS)            # explicit copy AT the boundary; without it
    cfg.update(overrides)           # update() writes into DEFAULTS forever
    return cfg

@dataclass(frozen=True)             # nothing to mutate, so rebinding is
class RequestCtx:                   # the only way to "change" it
    user_id: str
    tags: tuple[str, ...] = ()      # tuple, not list: no mutable field to leak

def with_user(ctx: RequestCtx, uid: str) -> RequestCtx:
    return replace(ctx, user_id=uid)   # NEW ctx; upstream keeps the old one

Break it: run the same += against a mutable and an immutable type.

xs = [1]; ys = xs; before = id(xs)
xs += [2]
print(id(xs) == before, ys)

n = 1; m = n; before = id(n)
n += 1
print(id(n) == before, m)
# look for: the list keeps its id and ys sees [1, 2]; the int gets a new id
# naive model predicts: both lines print the same, since += is just x = x + y

You get True [1, 2] then False 1. += is a request the type answers, so "does this line affect my caller?" can't be answered from syntax alone.

Interview

30-second answer: Neither: it's pass-by-object-reference. Python copies the reference into the parameter, so caller and callee hold two names for one object. Mutating it through the parameter is visible to the caller, because it's their object. Rebinding the parameter isn't, because that only overwrites the function's local slot. Assignment never copies; only copy(), deepcopy() or a constructor does.

Q · Mechanism — What does the interpreter do when it executes b = a? LOAD_FAST a pushes the pointer in a's slot onto the value stack, and STORE_FAST b pops it into b's slot and increments the refcount. Nothing is constructed. Inside a function the slots are fast-locals array entries; at module level they're dict keys. So binding is O(1) regardless of size, and the refcount ties names to lifetime: the object is freed at whichever rebind or scope exit drops the count to zero.

Q · Failure — A helper "tweaks a couple of defaults" on a config dict passed in, and later requests see corrupted config. What happened? The helper mutated the caller's dict instead of copying it. If that dict is a module-level singleton, the change lasts for the process. It's order-dependent, so the first request is fine and a later one that never called the helper breaks, pointing the stack trace somewhere innocent. Tests with one request miss it. Fix: copy at the boundary (dict(cfg), deepcopy if nested parts are mutated) or make the shared object immutable.

Q · Design — A request context is threaded through async handlers, and mutation-through-alias already caused an incident. Design its binding semantics. A shared mutable object passed through N handlers is a hidden global, and under asyncio an await lets another task observe half-applied changes. So make it immutable by construction: a frozen dataclass with tuple and frozenset fields, since a frozen dataclass still hands out a mutable list. Updates become ctx = replace(ctx, …), turning the chain into a pipeline. Per-task scratch state goes in a ContextVar. First signal to instrument: a dev middleware asserting id(ctx) is never reused across requests, which catches a module-level default instantly.

Compare

Operation Name Object Aliases see it?
b = a + [1] rebinds to a new object untouched
b.append(1) / b[0] = 9 unchanged mutated in place
b += [1] (list) rebinds to the same object mutated in place
b += 1 (int) rebinds to a new int untouched
del b unbound refcount −1, freed at zero

Pitfalls

  • "Python passes by value" or "by reference"
    It passes references by value: a new name bound to the same object.
    ↳ So: mutating the parameter shows in the caller; rebinding it (param = []) doesn't.
    ↳ Interview: say "by reference" and that's the next question.
  • "b = a gives me an independent copy"
    It's an alias: two names, one object.
    ↳ Symptom: b.append(x) changes what a shows.
    ↳ Fix: only an explicit copy or a constructor like list(a) makes a new object.
  • Not the same: rebinding, mutating, copying
    ↳ Difference: a line either rebinds a name (x = …) or mutates an object (x.append, x[0] = …); copying is always an explicit call.
    ↳ Use: naming which one a line does settles most aliasing bugs.
  • Don't "reset" a caller's list with param = [].
    ↳ Why: it only points your local name at a new list; the caller keeps the old one.
    ↳ Instead: param.clear(), and say in the signature that the function mutates its input.
  • Don't reach for deepcopy as the default defence.
    ↳ Why: it's O(whole graph), duplicates things you meant to share (caches, parents) and fails on locks and sockets.
    ↳ Instead: copy the one field that needs it, or make the data immutable.
  • Don't compare id() values in production code.
    ↳ Why: small ints and some strings are cached, and ids are reused after an object dies.
    ↳ Instead: is, and only against singletons like None.
  • 🔖 Version: binding semantics are language-defined and stable across Python 3.
    ↳ CPython-only: the opcodes that implement them (names shifted in 3.11–3.13); explain the model, not the opcodes.

Connections

Path:execution modelnames & bindingis vs == / mutable defaults / copy
  • Builds on the execution model: every value is a heap object, so a name can only ever hold a pointer.
  • Used by is vs ==: "same object?" only means something because names share objects.
  • Used by the mutable-default trap and copy semantics: one shared object seen through two names, and how to opt out.
  • Same mechanism as reference counting: every binding and rebinding moves a count.
  • Same idea elsewhere: Java and JavaScript object references; a C pointer you can't do arithmetic on.

notes.title: is vs ==, Identity & Interning
notes.html:
References

Identity comparisons (is) · id() · sys.intern · Real Python: is vs ==

TL;DR

== asks "same value?" and calls your code. is asks "same object?" and cannot be fooled, or reasoned with.

Flow:x is yIS_OP compares two pointers, runs no codesame object?
x == yCOMPARE_OPx.__eq__(y) ─NotImplementedy.__eq__(x) ─NotImplementedfalls back to identity

Recall

Prompt Answer
is compares? == compares? is → identity (same object); == → value, via __eq__.
Draw by hand: is vs == is: two arrows into one box. ==: two boxes, __eq__ compares contents. 256 shares one cached box.
Small-int cache range? −5 to 256, allocated once at startup (CPython detail).
Why is 257 is 257 inconsistent? One compilation unit folds the constants (True); separate units don't (False).
When is is correct? None, True, False, enum members, and sentinels you created.
== False but is True? n = float("nan"): n == n is False, n is n is True.

The idea

You think is is a stricter, faster ==. It's a different question, and CPython's caches make the wrong question return the right answer often enough to hide the bug:

a, b = [1, 2], [1, 2]
a == b, a is b        # → (True, False)   equal values, two objects
x = 256; y = 256
x is y                # → True            same shape, opposite answer
p = 257               # (separate REPL line)
q = 257
p is q                # → False

is did the same thing every time: it compared identities. What changed is which objects you were handed. In CPython, ints from −5 to 256 are created once at startup and reused, so two 256s are genuinely one object. 257 has no cache, so each REPL line builds its own.

Strings do the same with interning. Identifier-like literals are shared at compile time, but a string built at runtime is a new object:

s1 = "admin"; s2 = "".join(["ad", "min"])
s1 == s2, s1 is s2    # → (True, False)

And identity isn't just stricter equality. NaN runs the other way: n is n is True, n == n is False, because IEEE-754 says NaN equals nothing. The trade: is never lies about identity, but identity is almost never the question you meant, so reach for it only when "this exact object" is the semantics.

How it works

The two operators take different paths; the caches in the picture sit underneath object creation, not inside either operator:

The rules on each path:

Rule What actually happens
is runs no code IS_OP compares two PyObject * pointers: it can't be overridden and never raises. == can be made to lie: an __eq__ returning True makes Sneaky() == None true, while Sneaky() is None stays false (the eq / hash contract says what an honest __eq__ owes).
Constant folding is a second cache Within one compilation unit (a function body, a module, one exec), equal constants are stored once in co_consts. So two 257s in a script are one object, on separate REPL lines two: the answer depends on how the source was compiled, not on your logic.
id() is unique only among live objects Conceptually a constant for the object's lifetime; in CPython it's the address, reused once the object is freed, so a stored id() can match a newer object.
Python warns you Since 3.8, x is 257 or x is "admin" raises a compile-time SyntaxWarning: "is" with a literal.

Code

The broken check passes every unit test written with the literal. The sentinel is where identity is the semantics:

def is_admin_broken(role: str) -> bool:
    return role is "admin"            # SyntaxWarning since 3.8; false for JSON input

def is_admin(role: str) -> bool:
    return role == "admin"            # correct wherever the string came from

MISSING = object()                    # unique, unforgeable sentinel

def get(cfg: dict, key: str, default=MISSING):
    value = cfg.get(key, MISSING)
    if value is MISSING:              # identity is exactly the question here
        if default is MISSING:
            raise KeyError(key)
        return default
    return value

Break it: same value, two compilation strategies.

def same_unit():
    p = 257; q = 257
    return p is q
g = {}
exec("m = 257", g); exec("n = 257", g)
print(same_unit(), g["m"] is g["n"])
# look for: two different answers for the same value 257
# naive model predicts: one consistent answer either way

It prints True False (verified on CPython 3.9.6). The value never changed; only whether the compiler could fold both literals into one constant. Identity is a fact about allocation, so any check built on it is a check on CPython's memory behaviour.

Interview

30-second answer: == asks whether two objects have the same value, by calling __eq__. is asks whether they're the same object, a pointer check that runs no user code. Use == for values. Use is for None, because there's exactly one None and __eq__ can be overridden to lie. The trap is that CPython caches small ints and interns strings, so is on values sometimes works in tests.

Q · Mechanism — Why is 256 is 256 true but 257 is 257 sometimes false? CPython pre-allocates −5..256 at startup and returns the same object whenever one is produced, so is is true because they really are one object. It's a memory optimisation, not a language guarantee. Above that range the answer still wavers, because the compiler folds equal constants within one compilation unit: true inside one function, false across two REPL lines. That's why identity checks on non-singletons are never correct.

Q · Failure — Tests pass locally, but CI fails on assert record_id is expected_id. Diagnose. Someone used is for value equality. Local IDs fell inside the small-int cache, so both sides were the same object by luck; CI data crossed 256 and equal ints became distinct objects. The string form is worse and security-relevant: role is "admin" passes tests with an interned literal, then denies a real admin once role arrives from JSON. Fix both with ==, and fail CI on Ruff F632.

Q · Design — A dedup layer must decide "seen this?" across millions of events. When is identity right, and where does it break? Identity is right only for "this same live instance": a visited-set that breaks graph cycles, or a WeakSet of objects already processed. The binding constraint is lifetime: a long-lived set of raw id() values eventually matches a freed address reused by a new object, a false "seen" whose rate tracks GC pressure. Equal-but-distinct events must dedup together, which identity can't see, so hash a normalised payload into a set, or a Bloom filter or Redis at scale. Watch false-dedup rate against GC activity first.

Compare

is ==
Asks same object? same value?
Runs user code never; can't raise yes; may raise or lie
Correct for None, bools, enum members, sentinels everything else
Fails when caching makes it accidentally True __eq__ is written badly
NaN n is n → True n == n → False

Pitfalls

  • "is is just a faster =="
    It answers a different question: "same object?", not "same value?".
    ↳ Why it bites: it works until two equal values happen to be separate objects.
  • "is on equal strings is fine, strings are immutable"
    Immutability is irrelevant.
    ↳ Why: CPython only auto-interns compile-time, identifier-like literals; equal strings built at runtime are usually different objects.
  • "If a == b, then a is b might as well be true"
    Backwards: is implies == for sane types, never the reverse.
    ↳ Edge: NaN breaks even that: x is x but x != x, which is why containers check identity before equality.
  • Not the same as hashing
    ↳ Difference: identity is which object, equality is what value, and hash() must agree with __eq__, not id().
    ↳ Symptom: hash-by-identity + compare-by-value breaks dict and set lookups.
  • Don't use is on values from outside the process (JSON, sockets, DB rows).
    ↳ Why: they're built at runtime, so no caching or interning applies; sharing an object is random.
    ↳ Instead: == for values, is only for None and sentinels.
  • Don't store raw id() values to recognise an object later.
    ↳ Why: after garbage collection the address is reused, so a stale id matches a new object.
    ↳ Instead: hold a weakref.
  • 🔖 Version: the −5..256 cache, constant folding and interning are CPython details, not guarantees.
    ↳ Since 3.8: x is 5 with a literal raises a SyntaxWarning for exactly this reason.

Connections

Path:names & bindingis vs ==eq / hash contractdict internals
  • Builds on names & binding: "same object?" only matters because names share objects.
  • Used by the eq / hash contract: equal values with different identities must land in one dict slot.
  • Used by copy semantics: a copy is == to the original but never is it.
  • Same mechanism as str internals: interning is the string version of the small-int cache.
  • Same idea elsewhere: Java's == (reference) vs .equals() (value), with the same Integer cache trap for −128..127.

notes.title: Mutable vs Immutable & the Shared-Default Trap
notes.html:
References

Function definitions: default parameter values · Glossary: hashable · dataclasses.field(default_factory=…) · Ruff B006 mutable-argument-default · Real Python: Mutable vs immutable types

TL;DR

Defaults are evaluated once, at def-time, and stored on the function. Immutable default = shared and harmless. Mutable default = shared and permanent.

Flow:def runs[] evaluated onceMAKE_FUNCTION stores it in __defaults__every call that omits acc binds to that one listappends persist across calls

Recall

Prompt Answer
When is a default evaluated? Once, when the def statement executes, not per call.
Where does it live? On the function: f.__defaults__ (keyword-only: f.__kwdefaults__).
Why does def f(x, acc=[]) accumulate? Every default-using call binds to that one list; appends persist.
The fix? acc=None, then acc = [] if acc is None else acc.
Why not acc = acc or []? A caller's empty list is falsy and gets silently replaced.
Draw by hand: where the default lives Function object → __defaults__ → one list; every call's acc arrow points at it.

The idea

Where does the "hello" in def greet(name, greeting="hello") live between calls? On the function object, in greet.__defaults__ == ('hello',). So it was built before any call. A default that changes on evaluation shows exactly when:

import time
def stamp(t=time.time()): return t
stamp(); time.sleep(2); stamp()        # → same value twice

time.time() ran once, when def executed, because def is a statement that runs, not a declaration. So a default is one object, created at def-time and shared by every call that omits the argument.

That rule never changes. What changes is the type you put in the slot:

def collect(x, acc=[]):                 # ① [] built once  ② stored in __defaults__
    acc.append(x); return acc

collect(1); collect(2)                  # ③ → [1]  then ④ → [1, 2]

The string default was shared too, but nothing can alter a string. The worst a call can do is rebind its own local name. A list can be changed in place, so each call's append is permanent. The fix doesn't fight the rule. It puts something unmutatable in the slot and builds the real object in the body, which runs per call:

def collect(x, acc=None):
    acc = [] if acc is None else acc    # fresh list on every call

The trade: Python evaluates defaults once so calls stay cheap, and you own the decision of whether the stored default is something a caller could change.

How it works

The timing is visible in the bytecode of the enclosing scope, not the function body:

The rules behind ① to ④:

Rule What actually happens
Defaults are built by the enclosing scope In CPython the default expressions run as ordinary code where the def sits (①), and MAKE_FUNCTION attaches the results as __defaults__ (②). The body hasn't run and won't until someone calls it.
Call-time binding copies a pointer A missing argument binds the parameter to the object already in __defaults__ (③, ④): no re-evaluation, no copy. It's plain name binding with a longer fuse.
The shared default is process-lifetime state Never reset between calls, requests or test cases in one run, only by a fresh interpreter. Dataclasses refuse it: tags: list = [] raises ValueError when the class body runs.
Mutability belongs to the type Immutable types offer no in-place operation, so every "change" allocates and rebinds. That's also why they can promise a stable __hash__ (eq / hash contract).

Code

Three tools for three situations: the standard idiom, a private sentinel for when None is meaningful, and the dataclass form where the language enforces the fix:

from dataclasses import dataclass, field

_MISSING = object()                       # private sentinel, distinct from None

def add_tag(item, tags=None):             # ✅ the reflex idiom
    tags = [] if tags is None else tags   #    `is None`, never truthiness
    tags.append(item)
    return tags

def retry(fn, backoff=_MISSING):          # ✅ None MEANS "no backoff" here,
    if backoff is _MISSING:               #    so it can't double as "omitted"
        backoff = [1, 2, 4]
    return backoff

@dataclass
class Job:
    name: str
    tags: list[str] = field(default_factory=list)   # `= []` raises ValueError

Break it: watch the stored default's identity, then try the "clever" fix.

def collect(x, acc=[]):
    acc.append(x); return acc
for i in (1, 2, 3): print(id(collect.__defaults__[0]), collect(i))

def broken_fix(x, acc=None):
    acc = acc or []; acc.append(x); return acc
mine = []; broken_fix(1, mine); print(mine)
# look for: one constant id while the list grows; then mine stays empty
# naive model predicts: a new id per call, and mine == [1]

One id, growing [1] → [1, 2] → [1, 2, 3], and mine prints []. The caller's empty list is falsy, so or discarded it and appended to a different object. The fix introduced the same class of bug.

Interview

30-second answer: Default values are evaluated once, when def executes, and stored in f.__defaults__. Every call that omits the argument binds to that same object. With an immutable default that's harmless. With a list or dict, every mutation persists across calls. The fix is a None default and acc = [] if acc is None else acc in the body. Linters flag it as Ruff B006.

Q · Mechanism — Where does the default physically live, and why does that explain the trap? The enclosing scope evaluates each default and MAKE_FUNCTION stores the results as a tuple on the function: __defaults__ for positional parameters, __kwdefaults__ for keyword-only ones. At call time, a missing argument copies that pointer into the local slot. There's no re-evaluation and no copy. You can watch id(f.__defaults__[0]) stay constant while the list grows. Immutable defaults are shared exactly the same way; there's simply no operation that alters them.

Q · Failure — def fetch(key, _cache={}) passes tests but leaks memory and returns cross-tenant data in production. Diagnose. _cache is one dict shared for the process lifetime: an undeclared, unbounded global cache. It grows until the worker is OOM-killed, and a key that collides across tenants serves one tenant's value to another. Tests miss both, because short runs never grow the dict and single-tenant fixtures never cross. If sharing wasn't intended, use the None sentinel. If it was, make it explicit and bounded: lru_cache(maxsize=N) or a real cache keyed on the tenant.

Q · Design — Mutable-default bugs have shipped twice. Design guardrails so the class can't reach production. The bug beats review (the broken signature reads more naturally) and beats tests (one call behaves correctly), so the control must be mechanical. Fail CI on Ruff B006, don't just warn. Codify is None in the style guide with the or [] anti-fix called out. Standardise one shared _MISSING sentinel. Push boundary types toward frozen dataclasses and tuples so an accidental shared default raises instead of accumulating. Genuine shared state must be a named, bounded component. First alert: worker RSS growing without matching request volume.

Compare

Immutable (int, str, tuple, frozenset) Mutable (list, dict, set, most objects)
In-place change impossible; ops return new objects yes; methods mutate the same object
Safe as a default always unless sharing is the intent
Hashable (if contents are) __hash__ is None
+= rebinds to a new object mutates in place (__iadd__)
Dataclass field x: int = 0 field(default_factory=list)

Pitfalls

  • "Defaults are re-created on each call"
    Evaluated once, at def-time, and stored in __defaults__.
    ↳ Why: every call that omits the argument gets that same object.
    ↳ Check: func.__defaults__ shows the shared object in one line.
  • "x=[] is fine as long as I never reassign x"
    Reassigning is harmless; mutating is the bug.
    ↳ Why: x = … only rebinds a local name, but x.append changes the shared default.
    ↳ Symptom: the next call starts with the previous call's data.
  • "A tuple default is always safe"
    A tuple freezes references, not what they point to.
    ↳ Why: x=([],) still shares one inner list across calls.
    ↳ Symptom: appending to x[0] leaks state exactly like a list default.
  • Not the same as hashability
    ↳ Difference: a default is safe if it can't be mutated, not if it's hashable.
    ↳ Example: a hashable class can carry mutable fields; a tuple holding a list is immutable in shape but unhashable.
  • Don't use a mutable default as a cache.
    ↳ Why: it grows without bound, has no eviction, hides in the signature and is shared by every caller and test.
    ↳ Instead: functools.lru_cache(maxsize=…) or an explicit cache object.
  • Don't use None as the sentinel when None is a valid argument.
    ↳ Why: you can't tell "omitted" from "explicitly None".
    ↳ Instead: a private _MISSING = object(), compared with is.
  • 🔖 Version: def-time evaluation is stable across all of Python 3.
    ↳ Don't confuse: PEP 649 (3.14) made annotations lazy, not defaults.

Connections

Path:names & bindingmutable defaultseq / hash contractdataclasses
  • Builds on names & binding: the call binds a name to the stored object; nothing is copied.
  • Contrasts with closures' late binding: a default is read once at def time; a closure variable is read at every call.
  • Used by the eq / hash contract: immutable state is what keeps a hash stable.
  • Used by dataclasses: field(default_factory=list) is this fix built into the language.
  • Same idea elsewhere: Ruby and JavaScript re-evaluate defaults per call, which is why this trap surprises people coming from them.

notes.title: The Data Model / Dunder Protocols
notes.html:
References

Data model · Special method lookup · object.__new__ · functools.total_ordering · Real Python: Python's magic methods

TL;DR

Syntax is a call: the interpreter reads a slot on the TYPE and dispatches to a dunder. Define the dunder and you get the syntax, and the protocol's other obligations with it.

Flow:len(x) / x + yread the slot on type(x), never x.__dict__filled: call your dunderbinary op missing or NotImplemented: try type(y).__radd__(x)neither answers: TypeError

Recall

Prompt Answer
Where are dunders looked up? On the type; the instance __dict__ is skipped entirely.
__new__ vs __init__? __new__ allocates and returns the instance; __init__ fills it, returns None.
__repr__ vs __str__? repr for developers, str for users. str falls back to repr, never reverse.
Define __eq__ alone? Python sets __hash__ = None; the class becomes unhashable.
__eq__ on an unknown type returns? NotImplemented, not False, so the other operand gets a turn.
Draw by hand: how x + y reaches your code slot on type(x) → your __add__ → NotImplemented? → type(y).__radd__ → else TypeError.

The idea

Why does writing a method with underscores around its name change what + or len() does? Start with a class that has none:

class Money:
    def __init__(self, cents): self.cents = cents
a, b = Money(100), Money(100)
a            # → <__main__.Money object at 0x7f3c…>
a == b       # → False      (inherited from object: identity)
len(a)       # → TypeError: object of type 'Money' has no len()

That's the default. object supplies one generic answer per question it can answer: the address for display, identity for equality, nothing for length. Those answers live on the type, not the instance. Now add two methods and call nothing new:

    def __repr__(self): return f"Money({self.cents})"
    def __eq__(self, other):
        return isinstance(other, Money) and self.cents == other.cents
a, a == b    # → (Money(100), True)
{a}          # → TypeError: unhashable type: 'Money'

repr(a) and a == b are syntax, yet defining methods changed them. The interpreter has a fixed table from syntax to dunder names and looks them up on your type:

The unasked-for change is the obligation: defining __eq__ removed the inherited hash, because identity hashing would now contradict your equality (see eq-hash-contract).

The trade: implementing a protocol method buys your object a piece of built-in syntax, and the data model holds you to that protocol's other obligations whether you noticed them or not.

How it works

Every operator and built-in takes the same path to your code:

The rules along that path:

Rule What actually happens
Dunders are type slots In CPython each dunder maps to a C function pointer on the type object: __repr__ → tp_repr, __hash__ → tp_hash, __eq__/__lt__ → tp_richcompare, __add__ → nb_add, __len__ → mp_length. len(x) calls the slot, with no attribute lookup for "__len__".
Lookup skips the instance The docs call it implicit special method lookup (see the picture). The reason is speed: every + in a loop would otherwise pay a full MRO walk.
Binary operators get a reflected turn If type(x).__add__ is missing or returns NotImplemented, Python tries type(y).__radd__(x). That's how 2 * vector works when int has never heard of your class.
Construction is the same idea, one level up Money(100) calls type.__call__: __new__ allocates and returns an instance, then __init__ runs on it only if it's a Money (class creation is the level above). Immutable types customise __new__; a singleton's __init__ still re-runs every call.

Code

A value object implements a coherent protocol surface, not a scattering of dunders:

import functools

@functools.total_ordering                  # synthesises <=, >, >= from __eq__ + __lt__
class Money:
    __slots__ = ("cents",)                 # value objects are high-count

    def __init__(self, cents: int) -> None:
        self.cents = cents
    def __repr__(self) -> str:             # round-trips: eval(repr(m)) == m
        return f"Money({self.cents})"
    def __eq__(self, other: object) -> bool:
        if not isinstance(other, Money):
            return NotImplemented          # NOT False: let the other type answer
        return self.cents == other.cents
    def __lt__(self, other: "Money") -> bool:
        return self.cents < other.cents
    def __hash__(self) -> int:             # restored; same field as __eq__
        return hash(self.cents)

In new code, @dataclass(frozen=True, order=True, slots=True) generates the same surface correctly; hand-write it only when equality isn't "compare fields in order" (currency-aware money, pre-release versions).

Break it: attach a dunder to an instance, then to the class.

class Box: pass
b = Box()
b.__len__ = lambda: 5
print(b.__len__())        # explicit call: ordinary attribute lookup
try: len(b)
except TypeError as e: print(e)
Box.__len__ = lambda self: 7
print(len(b))
# look for: explicit call works, len() raises, then len() returns the CLASS's 7
# naive model predicts: len(b) is 5, because b clearly has a __len__

You get 5, object of type 'Box' has no len(), then 7 with the instance attribute still present. len() never looked at b, which is why Mock needs MagicMock to fake len and __enter__, and why __getattr__ can't rescue a missing protocol method.

Interview

30-second answer: The data model is the interpreter's published interface: a fixed list of dunder names it calls on your type in exchange for letting your objects use syntax like +, len, for and with. Lookup goes through type slots and skips the instance. Define __repr__ on everything, since str falls back to it. And defining __eq__ removes __hash__ unless you restore it.

Q · Mechanism — What happens when Python evaluates len(x), and why doesn't setting x.__len__ work? Defining __len__ in the class body makes class creation write the function into the type's length slot. len(x) reads that slot on type(x) and calls it, with no string lookup. An instance attribute lives in x.__dict__, which the slot read never consults, so len(x) still raises while x.__len__() works as a normal attribute call. The motivation is speed; the consequence is that protocols can't be patched per object.

Q · Failure — A value object sorts inconsistently and misbehaves in a set. The team hand-wrote __eq__ and __lt__. What broke? Two things. Hashing: __eq__ alone sets __hash__ = None, and a hand-added hash over different fields makes equal objects miss in sets (see 04a). Ordering: only __lt__ exists, so sorted() works and >= raises, and behaviour depends on which operator the algorithm uses. Tests using sorted() pass. Fix: @total_ordering, a hash over exactly the __eq__ fields, or a frozen=True, order=True dataclass.

Q · Design — Design a value-object layer (money, coordinates, versions) used as dict keys, sorted, and sent across services. The binding constraint is key usage, so equality and hash must derive from fields that can't change: @dataclass(frozen=True, order=True, slots=True). __repr__ round-trips for debugging, but the wire format belongs to an explicit serializer, never __str__, or a log-format tweak becomes a wire change. Overload arithmetic only where the domain is arithmetic: Money + Money yes, Version + Version no. Watch first for a mutable field sneaking into hashed state; a CI test asserting the type is frozen catches it.

Compare

Concern Dunder(s) Triggered by Obligation
Construction __new__, __init__ Cls(...) __new__ returns the instance; __init__ returns None
Display __repr__, __str__ repr()/containers; print()/f-strings str falls back to repr
Equality / hash __eq__, __hash__ ==, in, dict/set __eq__ removes __hash__
Ordering __lt__ … __ge__ <, sorted, heapq all four, or one + @total_ordering
Operators __add__, __radd__ … +, * NotImplemented for unknown types
Container __len__, __getitem__, __iter__, __contains__ len, x[i], for, in __getitem__ alone makes it iterable

Pitfalls

  • "__init__ is the constructor"
    __new__ creates the object; __init__ sets up one that exists.
    ↳ Why it matters: immutables (int, tuple subclasses) and singletons must do their work in __new__; by __init__ the value is fixed.
  • "Defining __str__ is enough"
    Backwards: define __repr__ first.
    ↳ Why: str() falls back to __repr__, never the reverse, and logs, debuggers and containers use repr.
  • Not the same as inheritance
    ↳ Difference: protocol behaviour comes from the special methods a type defines (CPython: filled type slots), not its place in a hierarchy.
    ↳ Example: any class with __len__ and __getitem__ acts like a sequence without subclassing.
  • Don't override __new__ when __init__ would do.
    ↳ Why: Python calls __init__ on whatever __new__ returns if it's an instance of the class.
    ↳ Symptom: a __new__-based singleton gets re-initialised and loses its state.
  • Don't write half an ordering, or clever operators.
    ↳ Why: only __lt__ makes >= raise; a + with side effects costs every reader a trip to the source.
    ↳ Instead: @total_ordering, and boringly mathematical operators.
  • Don't supply a dunder via __getattr__ or an instance attribute.
    ↳ Why: implicit lookup (len(x), x + y) goes straight to the type and skips both.
    ↳ Symptom: the method "exists" in a REPL but the operator still fails.
  • 🔖 Version: dataclass(slots=True) and kw_only are 3.10+; list[int] generics 3.9+.
    ↳ Note: slot names like tp_repr are CPython detail, an explanation, not a guarantee.

Connections

Path:execution modeldunder protocolseq / hash contract / slots / truthiness / ordering
  • Builds on is vs ==: the inherited __eq__ is identity until you define one.
  • Used by the eq / hash contract: the protocol pair with the strictest obligation.
  • Used by the iterator protocol: iter() and next() are this same type-slot lookup.
  • Contrasts with attribute lookup: ordinary x.name does check the instance; implicit dunder lookup doesn't.
  • Same idea elsewhere: C++ operator overloading and Kotlin's operator fun, both resolved on the type.

notes.title: The __eq__ / __hash__ Contract
notes.html:
References

Data model: object.__hash__ · Data model: object.__eq__ · Glossary: hashable · PYTHONHASHSEED · Real Python: Build a hash table

TL;DR

__hash__ is an index over __eq__: hash picks the region, == confirms the match. Equal ⟹ same hash (required). Same hash ⟹ nothing (a legal collision). The hash must not change while the object is in a container.

Flow:x in shash(x) picks where to look__eq__ confirms each candidate thereso equal objects must hash equaland a hashed field must not change while the object is inside

Recall

Prompt Answer
The contract in one line? a == b ⟹ hash(a) == hash(b). The converse is not required.
Define __eq__ alone — what happens? Python sets __hash__ = None; the class is unhashable and fails loud.
Draw by hand: the mutated key k stored in the slot for hash(1); after k.n = 2 the lookup probes hash(2)'s slot, finds nothing: in is False.
Why not hash a mutable field? Placement happens once at insert; mutation strands the object in the wrong slot.
What's wrong with return 0? Contract-correct, but one probe chain: O(n) per op, O(n²) to build.
Is hash("abc") stable across processes? No — str/bytes hashing is salted per process (default since 3.3).

The idea

Why can you put a plain object in a set when you never wrote __hash__? Because both defaults come from object, and both mean identity:

class Point:                       # ① no __eq__: identity hash inherited
    def __init__(self, x, y): self.x, self.y = x, y

a, b = Point(1, 2), Point(1, 2)
a == b, hash(a) == hash(b)     # → (False, False)  both ask "same object?"

The two can never disagree, so the default is safe. Now do the natural thing for a value object and redefine equality:

    def __eq__(self, o): return isinstance(o, Point) and (self.x, self.y) == (o.x, o.y)   # ② __eq__, no __hash__

Point(1, 2) == Point(1, 2)     # → True
{Point(1, 2)}                  # ③ → TypeError: unhashable type: 'Point'

Python noticed that __eq__ now asks "same value?" while the inherited hash still asks "same object?", so it set __hash__ = None. Had the identity hash survived, Point(1, 2) in {Point(1, 2)} would print False: equal, present, and not found, with no error. Python judges an unusable class better than a silently wrong one. The fix (④) is def __hash__(self): return hash((self.x, self.y)), which hashes the same fields __eq__ compares.

The trade: you may define what equality means for your type, and in exchange hashing must answer the same question.

The half Python does not catch is changing a hashed field after insertion:

How it works

Python decides your class's hash once, when the class body runs (verified on CPython 3.12). The lookup itself, hash then probe then __eq__, belongs to dict internals:

The rules the contract rests on:

Rule What actually happens
Hashing narrows; equality decides The hash only reaches the right neighbourhood of an open-addressing table, and __eq__ confirms the candidate. So the contract is one-directional: equal objects must hash equal, while unequal objects sharing a hash are a collision __eq__ resolves.
The hash must be stable while inside Placement is decided once, at insertion, and nothing re-hashes on mutation, so a changed hashed field strands the object (the picture, and Break it).
A constant hash is correct and ruinous return 0 satisfies the contract, but every key shares one probe chain: lookup degrades from O(1) average to O(n), and building a set of N objects does O(n²) work.
str/bytes hashes are salted per process PYTHONHASHSEED randomises them at startup (default since 3.3) against collision DoS, so two workers or two restarts disagree on hash("abc").

Code

Hand-write the pair only when equality isn't "all fields". Otherwise let a frozen dataclass generate both from one field list, so they can't drift:

from dataclasses import dataclass

@dataclass(frozen=True, slots=True)   # frozen ⇒ __hash__ generated from the same
class CacheKey:                       # fields as __eq__; mutation raises
    tenant: str                       # FrozenInstanceError instead of corrupting
    resource: str
    version: int

class CaseInsensitiveKey:             # hand-written: equality is NOT "all fields"
    __slots__ = ("name",)
    def __init__(self, name): self.name = name
    def __eq__(self, o):
        if not isinstance(o, CaseInsensitiveKey):
            return NotImplemented     # let the other operand try
        return self.name.casefold() == o.name.casefold()
    def __hash__(self):
        return hash(self.name.casefold())   # SAME normalisation __eq__ uses

Break it: mutate a hashed field after insertion, the half Python does not protect you from.

class Key:
    def __init__(self, n): self.n = n
    def __eq__(self, o): return isinstance(o, Key) and self.n == o.n
    def __hash__(self): return hash(self.n)

k = Key(1); s = {k}
k.n = 2                                   # mutate the hashed field
print(k in s, any(x is k for x in s), len(s))
# look for: the object is provably inside while `in` says it isn't
# naive model predicts: True True 1

It prints False True 1. Placement used hash(1), and the lookup now probes from hash(2), a region that was never written. frozen=True turns this silent corruption into an exception at the mutation.

Interview

30-second answer: Objects that compare equal must return equal hashes. The converse isn't required, because collisions are legal. Dicts and sets hash to find a region, then use __eq__ to confirm, so an equal object that hashes elsewhere is never found. Membership lies and dedup keeps duplicates, with no error. That's why defining __eq__ alone makes a class unhashable, and why @dataclass(frozen=True) is the safe default.

Q · Mechanism — Why does defining __eq__ make a class unhashable? A custom __eq__ almost certainly changed what equality means, so the inherited identity hash from object is now inconsistent with it. Rather than let a silent contract violation ship, Python sets __hash__ = None in that class body, and the first dict or set insertion raises TypeError. It turns a silent data bug into a loud one at the earliest possible moment. You opt back in by defining a __hash__ over the fields __eq__ compares.

Q · Failure — testing: catching the quadratic unprompted. A team returned a constant from __hash__ to "just make it work" in a set. Consequence? It satisfies the contract and turns the table into one probe chain: O(n) per operation, O(n²) to build. With the handful of objects a unit test uses, it's invisible. At production volume, a dedup pass silently goes quadratic and shows up as a timeout in code that hasn't changed, so the investigation starts in the wrong place. Fix: hash exactly the immutable fields __eq__ compares, and freeze them.

Q · Design — A cache keyed on (tenant, resource, version) objects shows falling hit rate and climbing memory. How do you reason about it? That pair is a signature. Every lookup that misses its prior entry counts as a miss and inserts a duplicate. A capacity problem shows falling hits with flat memory. Suspect __eq__/__hash__ drift (a field added to one but not the other) or a mutated key field. Make the key @dataclass(frozen=True) and add a property test that a == b ⟹ hash(a) == hash(b). For a distributed cache, never key on hash(), since it's salted per process. Use a versioned canonical serialisation, shortened with hashlib.blake2b if needed. Watch entry count against distinct logical keys.

Compare

Situation __eq__ __hash__ Result
Neither defined identity from id() hashable, equality = identity
__eq__ only value None (automatic) unhashable, fails loud
Both, same fields value value correct key
Both, different fields value value silent corruption
@dataclass(frozen=True) generated generated correct by construction
@dataclass (unfrozen, eq=True) generated None unhashable, same rule

Pitfalls

  • "Unequal objects must have different hashes"
    Only equal ⟹ equal hash is required; collisions are allowed.
    ↳ Tell: stating it backwards is the fastest sign of a shaky model, and leads to over-engineered hashes.
  • "Adding __eq__ leaves hashing alone"
    It sets __hash__ = None (Python 3).
    ↳ Symptom: instances become unhashable and fail as dict keys or set members; Python 2 didn't do this, so older material skips it.
  • "Hashable means safe as a dict key"
    Hashability is the type's; stability is your usage.
    ↳ Why: mutate a hashed field after insertion and the dict looks in the wrong bucket: the key is effectively lost (see Break it).
  • Not the same as immutability
    ↳ Difference: the contract covers only the fields equality and hashing use.
    ↳ Example: hashable objects can hold mutable unhashed fields; an immutable tuple containing a list is unhashable.
  • Don't "fix" unhashability with __hash__ = lambda self: 0.
    ↳ Why: it's legal, but every instance lands in one bucket and lookups degrade from O(1) to O(n).
    ↳ Result: a loud error traded for a slow one that only shows at scale.
  • Don't make a mutable entity hashable just to fit a set.
    ↳ Instead: a WeakSet, a dict keyed on a stable ID, or a frozen snapshot: each ties the hash to something that can't change.
  • 🔖 Version: str/bytes hash randomisation (PYTHONHASHSEED) is on by default since 3.3.
    ↳ So: never rely on hash values or set order across runs; frozen=True is 3.7+, slots=True 3.10+.

Connections

Path:dunder protocolseq / hash contractdict internals / set internals
  • Builds on dunder protocols: __eq__ and __hash__ are two slots on the type that must agree.
  • Builds on mutability: only immutable state keeps a hash stable.
  • Used by dict internals: the probe sequence that relies on this contract.
  • Used by ordering & sorting and lru_cache: sorting is the equality side's sibling, and cache keys are dict keys.
  • Same idea elsewhere: Java's equals() / hashCode() contract, with the same "mutable key in a HashSet" bug.

notes.title: __slots__ & Instance Layout
notes.html:
References

Data model: __slots__ · sys.getsizeof · Real Python: Using __slots__

TL;DR

__dict__ = dynamic attribute storage, decided at runtime. __slots__ = fixed attribute storage, decided at class creation.

Flow:class body lists __slots__each name becomes a member descriptor on the classinstances get fixed value cells, no __dict__u.name goes descriptoroffset, no hashingan undeclared name has nowhere to go: AttributeError

Recall

Prompt Answer
What does __slots__ remove? The per-instance __dict__ and default __weakref__; values stored inline.
What is a slot, mechanically? A member descriptor on the class pointing at a fixed offset in the instance.
Inheritance gotcha? A subclass without its own __slots__ silently regains a __dict__.

The idea

When you write self.name = name, where does the string physically go? By default, into a dict that hangs off the instance:

class User:
    def __init__(self, name, age): self.name = name; self.age = age
u = User("Raje", 30)
u.__dict__            # → {'name': 'Raje', 'age': 30}
u.company = "Acme"    # → accepted: it's just another dict key

Every instance pays for its own hash table, and every read hashes the name and probes it. Add one line and the dict disappears:

class User:
    __slots__ = ("name", "age")
    def __init__(self, name, age): self.name = name; self.age = age
u = User("Raje", 30)
u.company = "Acme"    # → AttributeError: 'User' object has no attribute 'company'
u.__dict__            # → AttributeError: absent, not empty

You specified the instance layout by hand instead of taking the general-purpose dict. The trade: you give up inventing attributes at runtime and get back the dict's memory on every instance plus a cheaper lookup on every access.

How it works

Each slot is a member descriptor. In CPython, class creation turns every listed name into a descriptor on the class that knows its value's byte offset inside an instance (User.name → <member 'name' of 'User' objects>). The class holds the map; the instance holds only values.

Data descriptors win lookup. Reading u.name walks the MRO for a data descriptor. A default class has none, so it falls back to u.__dict__["name"]; a slotted class hits the member descriptor and reads the offset, no hashing. An undeclared name has neither, so assignment raises.

The layout belongs to one class, not the hierarchy. Each class declares its own layout, so any class in the MRO that omits __slots__ reintroduces a __dict__ for its instances (see Break it). Slotting also drops __weakref__ unless you list it, which matters for weak references.

Code

Measured on CPython 3.10, re-verified on 3.9.6 with identical figures:

import sys
from dataclasses import dataclass

class Point:
    def __init__(self, x, y): self.x = x; self.y = y
class SlotPoint:
    __slots__ = ("x", "y")
    def __init__(self, x, y): self.x = x; self.y = y

p, s = Point(1, 2), SlotPoint(1, 2)
print(sys.getsizeof(p) + sys.getsizeof(p.__dict__))   # → 152  (48 + 104)
print(sys.getsizeof(s))                               # → 48   (~104 B saved)

@dataclass(slots=True)             # 3.10+: the default way to write it now
class Point3:
    x: int
    y: int

Break it: leave __slots__ off one subclass.

class Base:  __slots__ = ("a",)
class Child(Base): pass            # no __slots__ declared
print(hasattr(Base(), "__dict__"), hasattr(Child(), "__dict__"))
Child().whatever = 1               # does this raise?
# look for: Base has no __dict__, but Child silently gets one back
# naive model predicts: False False, and the assignment raises

It prints False True and the assignment succeeds. Nothing breaks and no test fails; the saving is simply gone. Adding __slots__ = () to Child flips it back.

Interview

30-second answer: Instances normally keep attributes in a per-instance __dict__: flexible, but a hash table per object and a lookup per read. __slots__ declares a fixed attribute set, and CPython stores the values inline behind member descriptors on the class. The win is mostly memory, about 104 bytes per two-field instance on 3.10. The costs: no undeclared attributes, no weakrefs unless you slot __weakref__.

Q · Mechanism — 50M small records, tight RSS budget. Do slots fit, and where do they stop being the answer? Dropping a ~104-byte dict each is roughly 5 GB, so yes: slot the whole hierarchy and assert not hasattr(obj, "__dict__") in CI. But fields stay boxed PyObjects (an int is ~28 bytes), so for uniform bulk data a columnar layout (NumPy, Arrow) beats slots by a wide margin.

Compare

Default __dict__ __slots__
Storage per-instance hash table inline slots + class descriptors
Undeclared attribute allowed AttributeError
Size, 2 fields (3.10) ~152 B 48 B
weakref unless "__weakref__" slotted

Pitfalls

  • "Slots make attribute access dramatically faster"
    The headline win is memory: no per-instance __dict__.
    ↳ So: slots pay off with very many instances, not as a general speed trick.
  • "Slotting the base class slots the hierarchy"
    Every class in the MRO must declare __slots__, often = ().
    ↳ Symptom: one subclass without it brings __dict__ back on every instance (see Break it).
  • Not the same as immutability or privacy
    ↳ Difference: slots fix which attribute names can exist; values stay freely writable.
    ↳ Bonus: a typo like obj.vaule = 1 raises instead of silently creating an attribute.
  • Don't slot classes with few instances or dynamic attributes.
    ↳ Why: the saving is per instance, and monkey-patching, some ORMs and serialisers need __dict__.
    ↳ Also: two parents with non-empty slots can't be combined: a layout conflict.
  • Don't forget __weakref__ if instances must be weakly referenced.
    ↳ Symptom: weakref.ref(obj) raises TypeError, usually far from the class, in a cache or observer.
  • 🔖 Version: sizes depend on CPython version, platform and attribute count; re-measure with sys.getsizeof.
    ↳ Since 3.10: @dataclass(slots=True); before that, __slots__ by hand.

Connections

Path:dunder protocolsslotsdescriptorsobject header
  • Builds on descriptors: a slot is a data descriptor, which is why it beats the instance dict in lookup.
  • Used by dataclasses: @dataclass(slots=True) writes the __slots__ for you.
  • Contrasts with the object header: slots trim the per-instance dict, never the fixed header every object pays.
  • Breaks when combined with weak references: no __weakref__ slot, no weakref, unless you list it.
  • Same idea elsewhere: a C struct or a Java class's fixed fields, versus a JavaScript object's open property bag.

notes.title: Copy Semantics (assignment vs shallow vs deep)
notes.html:
References

copy — shallow and deep copy operations · Pickle: __reduce__ / __getstate__ · Real Python: Shallow vs deep copying

TL;DR

Assignment copies nothing. Shallow copies the container. Deep copies the graph. The bug is always at the level you did not copy.

Flow:b = a copies nothingcopy.copy(a) builds a new outer container holding the same inner objectscopy.deepcopy(a) walks the whole graph with a memo keyed by id()a new object at every mutable level, shared references still shared

Recall

Prompt Answer
Assignment vs shallow vs deep? Alias · new outer, shared inner · new everything, recursively.
When does shallow bite? Nested mutables: mutating an inner object shows through both.
What does deepcopy's memo do? Maps id(original) → copy, so cycles stop and shared refs stay shared.

The idea

You think copy.copy gives you an independent object. It gives you a new container full of the same objects:

import copy
orig = [[1, 2], [3, 4]]
sh = copy.copy(orig)       # same as orig[:], list(orig)
dp = copy.deepcopy(orig)
sh is orig, sh[0] is orig[0]   # → (False, True)
orig[0].append(99)
sh, dp                     # → ([[1, 2, 99], [3, 4]], [[1, 2], [3, 4]])

Appending to sh itself would leave orig alone, so the shallow copy looks independent until someone mutates one level down. deepcopy kept going and built a new object at every level, so nothing is shared.

Cost scales the same way: shallow is O(top level), deep is O(reachable graph), happily duplicating a 200 MB cache hanging off one attribute. The trade: each rung buys independence one level deeper, and you pay by copying everything reachable from where you stop.

How it works

How deepcopy walks the graph (all four verified on CPython 3.12):

Rule What actually happens
It's graph traversal with a memo A naive recursion would loop forever on a self-referencing structure and split one object reached by two paths into two copies. A memo dict keyed by id() of each original, valued by its copy, fixes both: on a hit it returns the existing copy.
Register before recursing Each new copy goes into the memo before its children are copied, so a back-reference finds the in-progress copy and stops, and two paths to one object resolve to one copy (identity is the key).
Immutable leaves aren't copied Ints, strings and tuples of immutables come back as the same object: nothing observable depends on their identity, so the recursion bottoms out there.
Classes can opt out per field __copy__ and __deepcopy__(self, memo) override the defaults; without them copy falls back on the pickle protocol (__reduce_ex__) to rebuild the object.

Code

The hook matters for objects holding something uncopyable (connections, sockets, locks), where you choose per field what's duplicated and what's shared:

import copy

class Session:
    def __init__(self, user, conn):
        self.user, self.conn, self.tags = user, conn, []

    def __deepcopy__(self, memo):
        new = Session(self.user, self.conn)          # conn deliberately SHARED
        memo[id(self)] = new                         # register BEFORE recursing,
        new.tags = copy.deepcopy(self.tags, memo)    # or a cycle through tags loops
        return new

cfg = {"limits": {"rps": 10}, "name": "svc"}
shallow = dict(cfg)                  # inner dict shared
shallow["limits"]["rps"] = 99        # ⚠️ mutates cfg too
deep = copy.deepcopy(cfg)            # fully independent

Interview

30-second answer: A shallow copy makes a new top-level object filled with references to the same children, so the containers are distinct but nested mutation shows through both. copy.copy, slicing, list() and dict() all do this. A deep copy recursively copies the whole reachable graph, so nothing is shared. It costs the size of the graph and uses a memo dict to handle cycles and shared references.

Q · Mechanism — How does deepcopy survive cycles and copy shared references correctly? It threads a memo dict keyed by id(original). Before copying, it checks the memo and reuses any existing copy. Each object is registered before its children are copied, so a back-reference into a cycle finds the in-progress copy and stops. The same lookup means an object reached by two paths maps to one copy, so the result keeps the original's sharing shape instead of drifting into two independent objects.

Compare

b = a copy.copy / a[:] / dict(a) copy.deepcopy
New outer alias
New inner shared recursive
Cycles / shared refs n/a n/a via memo
Cost O(1) O(top level) O(reachable graph)
Hook — __copy__ __deepcopy__(self, memo)

Pitfalls

  • "copy.copy gives an object I can mutate freely"
    Only the top level is new; nested lists, dicts and objects are shared.
    ↳ Symptom: mutate a nested item and both copies change.
  • "lst[:] or dict(d) makes a deep copy"
    Both are shallow, exactly like copy.copy.
    ↳ So: safe for flat immutable values, unsafe once the values are mutable.
  • Not the same as assignment
    ↳ Difference: shallow and deep copies create new objects; assignment creates none, it adds a name.
    ↳ Use: name the rung (alias, shallow, deep) to explain any "why did both change?" bug.
  • Don't reach for deepcopy by default.
    ↳ Why: it walks the whole graph, so one attribute pointing at a cache or parent becomes a huge duplication.
    ↳ Instead: copy only the field that needs independence.
  • Don't deepcopy objects holding connections, sockets, files or locks.
    ↳ Why: those can't be meaningfully duplicated: errors, or two objects fighting over one resource.
    ↳ Instead: a __deepcopy__ that shares them deliberately.
  • Don't copy where immutability would do.
    ↳ Instead: a frozen dataclass + dataclasses.replace() gives copy-with-changes at shallow cost, and nothing can mutate the shared parts.

Connections

Path:names & bindingcopy semanticscyclic GC
  • Builds on names & binding: assignment aliases, so copying is the explicit opt-out.
  • Builds on mutability: only mutable nested state ever needs copying.
  • Same mechanism as the cyclic GC: both walk an object graph and must survive cycles.
  • Used by dataclasses: replace() is a shallow copy with changes.
  • Same idea elsewhere: JavaScript's spread ({...obj}) is shallow and structuredClone is deep; Java's clone() is shallow by default.

notes.title: Truthiness & Operator Protocols
notes.html:
References

Truth value testing · Data model: object.__bool__

TL;DR

if x: asks the object "are you empty?", not "are you None?". __bool__ first, __len__ second, true by default.

Recall

Prompt Answer
How does bool(obj) decide? __bool__ if defined; else __len__ (0 → False); else True.
What do __contains__ / __call__ power? in membership; calling an instance as obj().
What is NotImplemented? Sentinel a binary dunder returns to defer to the reflected operand.

The idea

if x: calls bool(x), which asks the type in a fixed order: __bool__, then __len__ (zero is false), then default true. That's why 0, "", [], {} and None are falsy with no special-casing anywhere. So implement __len__ and your class is falsy when empty, for free. Define __bool__ only when truthiness and emptiness differ, like an empty but successful result. The same fill-the-slot rule drives in (__contains__) and obj() (__call__). A comparison or arithmetic dunder returns NotImplemented to hand off to the other operand before Python raises TypeError. The trade: a surprising __bool__ makes every if in your codebase surprising.

Code

class Cart:
    def __init__(self, items): self.items = items
    def __len__(self): return len(self.items)          # drives truthiness
    def __contains__(self, x): return x in self.items  # powers `in`
    def __call__(self): return sum(self.items)         # instance is callable

print(bool(Cart([10, 20])), 20 in Cart([10, 20]))      # → True True
print(bool(Cart([])), Cart([10, 20])())                # → False 30

notes.title: Equality, Ordering & Sorting
notes.html:
References

Sorting HOWTO · functools.cmp_to_key · Real Python: How to use sorted() and .sort()

TL;DR

Sorting asks one question, <, of a key you computed once per element. Stable means ties keep their input order, which is what lets you sort in passes.

Flow:sorted(xs, key=f)f called once per element (N calls)Timsort finds already-ordered runscompares keys with < onlymerges adjacent runs, ties taken from the leftstable result

Recall

Prompt Answer
key= vs a comparator? key runs N times; cmp_to_key runs on every comparison, O(N log N).
Is sorted stable, and why? Guaranteed: Timsort merges only adjacent runs and takes ties from the left.
Which dunder does sorting use? __lt__ only, never __eq__. Incomparable types raise TypeError.

The idea

You arrive from Java or C++ looking for a two-argument comparator. Python's answer is a function of one argument:

rows = [("eng", 90), ("sales", 90), ("eng", 70)]
sorted(rows, key=lambda r: (r[0], -r[1]))   # → [('eng', 90), ('eng', 70), ('sales', 90)]
sorted([1, "a"])                            # → TypeError: '<' not supported between 'str' and 'int'

key compares nothing. It maps each element to a value Python already knows how to order, and the sort compares those with < (the only dunder it ever calls). A tuple key gives a multi-level sort for free because tuples compare element by element, and -r[1] reverses one numeric field without reversing the others. With no total order across unrelated types, Python refuses to guess.

The sort is also stable, by language guarantee: sorted(["banana", "apple", "cherry", "date"], key=len) returns banana before cherry, both length 6, in input order.

The trade: you give up the generality of an arbitrary comparator and get N key calls instead of O(N log N) comparator calls, plus a stable order you can compose sorts on.

How it works

Rule What actually happens
Decorate, then sort Conceptually sorted computes key(x) for every element first: N calls however many comparisons follow (3 calls for 3 elements, verified on CPython 3.12). Timsort then compares the precomputed keys in C.
Timsort exploits real-world order In CPython it detects already-ordered runs, extends short ones with insertion sort and merges runs, so nearly-sorted input approaches O(n) (list internals has the run detail).
Stability is by construction It only merges runs adjacent in the input and, on a tie, takes from the left run, so equal elements never swap. reverse=True keeps that guarantee.
Stability enables multi-pass sorts Sort by the secondary key, then the primary: the stable primary pass keeps the secondary order inside each group. Needed when a descending field isn't numeric and can't be negated in a tuple key.

The multi-pass case, traced (verified on CPython 3.12): department descending, a string, then name ascending.

Step Call Result Why
input — raj·sales, bo·eng, cy·sales, ana·eng
pass 1 sorted(staff, key=name) ana·eng, bo·eng, cy·sales, raj·sales the secondary key first
pass 2 sorted(p1, key=dept, reverse=True) cy·sales, raj·sales, ana·eng, bo·eng ties keep pass 1's name order

Code

import functools

rows = [("eng", 90), ("sales", 90), ("eng", 70)]

# descending field that can't be negated (e.g. text)? two stable passes:
by_salary = sorted(rows, key=lambda r: r[1], reverse=True)   # secondary first
print(sorted(by_salary, key=lambda r: r[0]))                 # then primary
# → [('eng', 90), ('eng', 70), ('sales', 90)]   works for any key type

# genuinely relational logic, not expressible as a per-element key
print(sorted([23, 11, 45, 32],
             key=functools.cmp_to_key(lambda a, b: (a % 10) - (b % 10))))
# → [11, 32, 23, 45]

Interview

30-second answer: key= computes a key once per element, N calls, and Timsort compares those keys natively. A comparator runs your Python function on every comparison, O(N log N) calls. It's also more expressive: key=str.lower, key=len, or a tuple key for multi-level sorts. cmp_to_key is an adapter for genuinely relational logic. Sorting only calls <, and it's guaranteed stable.

Q · Mechanism — What makes Timsort stable, and how does that let you sort by multiple keys? It merges only runs adjacent in the input and breaks ties toward the left run, so equal elements can't swap. That's why stability is in the spec. To sort by primary then secondary, sort by secondary first, then primary; the stable second pass preserves secondary order within each primary group. A tuple key does it in one pass, but only when every descending field is numeric.

Compare

Approach Calls to your function Use when
key=fn N almost always
tuple key N multi-level, ascending or numeric-descending
two stable passes N per pass a descending field isn't numeric
cmp_to_key(cmp) O(N log N) truly relational comparison only

Pitfalls

  • "sorted isn't stable"
    It's guaranteed stable: equal items keep their input order.
    ↳ Use: multi-pass sorting (by name, then by department) relies on it.
  • "A comparator is the natural way to sort objects"
    key= is the idiom, and faster.
    ↳ Why: the key is computed once per element, not on every comparison; cmp_to_key adapts legacy code.
  • Not the same as equality
    ↳ Difference: sorting calls only __lt__, never __eq__.
    ↳ So: defining __eq__ does nothing for sorted; ties stay in input order.
  • Don't define only __lt__ and assume full ordering.
    ↳ Symptom: sorted works but a >= b raises TypeError, in some other code path.
    ↳ Instead: @functools.total_ordering, or no methods and a key=.
  • Don't re-sort to keep a changing collection ordered.
    ↳ Why: each insert costs O(n log n).
    ↳ Instead: heapq, bisect.insort, or sortedcontainers.
  • Don't sort just to get the top k.
    ↳ Why: sorting is O(n log n); min/max are O(n), heapq.nlargest(k, …) is O(n log k).

Connections

Path:eq / hash contractordering & sortinglist internals
  • Builds on dunder protocols: __lt__ is the one comparison sorting calls; @total_ordering fills in the rest.
  • Contrasts with the eq / hash contract: equality decides dict membership; ordering decides sort position, and sorting never calls __eq__.
  • Used by functools: cmp_to_key adapts an old comparator, at O(N log N) Python calls.
  • Same mechanism as list internals: list.sort is the same Timsort, in place.
  • Same idea elsewhere: Java's Comparator.comparing(...).thenComparing(...) is the key approach; Collections.sort is stable too.
